description:
This milestone focuses on expanding the design patterns repository with three critical contributions:

Common Smart Contract Footguns & Defensive Patterns

A section outlining common mistakes in Cardano smart contract development (e.g. state token smuggling / unauthenticated contract state).

Defensive coding patterns and validation techniques to mitigate each.

Merkle Patricia Forestry (MPF)

Documentation on how to leverage MPF structures for insertion, removal and membership proofs in onchain code; includes use-cases and patterns for abstraction.

Metaprogramming Utilities for Reusability

A collection of examples of smart contract utility functions showcasing higher-level abstractions and metaprogramming macros for safer and DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) contract logic.

All additions will follow the established format and organizational structure of the current Anastasia Labs Design Patterns repository.

description:
This milestone focuses on adding robust design patterns around protocol parameterization and event-driven architecture for smart contracts on Cardano. Key outputs include:

Proxy Pattern for Dynamic Parameters

Demonstration of the proxy contract design pattern that enables upgradability by referencing parameter UTxOs.

Reference implementations showcasing how on-chain scripts can dynamically respond to off-chain parameter updates.

Parameter Validation Architecture

A secure, reusable pattern to enforce that a given smart contract is a parameterized instance of some contract (which accepts parameters) in onchain code, and to apply validation logic on the specific parameters with which that contract was applied.

Reward Account Registration as Global Event Map

A pattern leveraging stake key registration to build decentralized global registries for one-time or recurring events.

Applications may include claim maps, airdrop whitelists, or participation registries.
title: Dynamic Parameterization & Event Map Design Patterns

description:
A. MVP Functional Deployment

Fully functional MVP deployed on Cardano testnet implementing all five features: private order placement via ZK commitments, ZK proof generation and on-chain verification, end-to-end matching and settlement, liquidation and position close-out logic, and integration with the Midnight privacy layer.

B. Front-Running Prevention Validation

Executable test scenarios attempting order sniping or reordering, demonstrating failed front-running attempts due to ZK commitments and settlement rules.

C. Privacy Enforcement Validation

Verification that sensitive order data (price, size, trader identity) is not visible in on-chain transactions and cannot be reconstructed from public state.

D. Final Documentation

Public final report summarizing system architecture, benchmarks, security analysis, lessons learned, and next-step roadmap.

E. Final Demonstration Artifacts

  • Public final demo video showing live MVP execution on Cardano testnet.

description:
The unhappy paths and the edge cases identified in the previous milestones are included in this Bifrost iteration, where malicious players, coordination problems and Cardano possible network saturation are correctly managed. Hardening, optimisations and tuning are part of this version.

While at this moment we cannot be sure we know all the possible unhappy paths, they surely include Bitcoin reorg attacks, SPO collusion scenarios, Watchtower censorship attempts and Cardano network saturation. These should be considered for the completion of this milestone.

This milestone deliver the new code adding it to the official repo (https://github.com/FluidTokens/ft-bifrost-bridge).

While speed is not a property that Bifrost is aiming, the hardening and optimisations consist of securing the SPO and Watchtower programs and finding the most efficient ways to execute the existing logic.

The outputs therefore are:

  • Code improvement: the unhappy paths and the edge cases identified in the previous milestones are included in this Bifrost iteration: Bitcoin reorg attacks, SPO collusion scenarios, Watchtower censorship attempts and Cardano network saturation
  • Hardening and optimization: consist of securing the SPO and Watchtower programs and finding the most efficient ways to execute the existing logic

▶Note to Reviewers — Clarification on Milestone Structure Update

Following the reviewers’ feedback and Catalyst program requirements, we restructured Milestone 1 and 2 to better align with the original proposal’s Milestone 1, which was originally designed as a two-month activity.

Under Catalyst rules, proposals with a total grant of 770,000 ADA must define five milestones plus one final milestone (six total).

Additionally, the Catalyst module specifies that the first milestone cannot exceed 75,000 ADA.

To comply with these requirements without altering the original intent or deliverables, we divided the original two-month milestone into:

  • Milestone 1: Identification, outreach, and securing initial commitments from 2–3 Japanese financial institutions and/or corporates as potential participants for ideation workshops.
  • Milestone 2: formal confirmations and onboarding of ≥3 corporates.

Together, Milestone 1 + 2 reproduce the exact scope and objectives of the original proposal’s Milestone 1 while ensuring full Catalyst compliance, verifiability, and month-by-month accountability.

acceptance_criteria:
1. ≥1 testnet policy; ≥1,000 tokens minted; metadata updatable.
  2. The signing script successfully pushes data to the Testnet; the system verifies that the data comes from the authorized PagoTIC admin wallet and rejects unauthorized signatures.
  3. ≥2 PayoutEvents are recorded on Testnet using Metadata Label 674, serving as immutable attestation that the off-chain Fiat payment occurred.
  4. Smoke run demonstrates the full path on testnet, and a Testnet Report is produced summarising: policy ID, number of minted tokens, number of Events, typical transaction fees and any known limitations; the report is stored in the repository and linked from the SOM.
  5. ≥30 tests passing; CI runs on each PR. all work items for this milestone in the public issue tracker are closed or marked “done” and linked to the relevant pull requests.
description:
1. Deployment of the CIP-68 Minting Policy and Reference Validator on Testnet to manage dynamic NFT lifecycle (minting and metadata updates).
  2. Testnet PagoTIC - IncomeEvent: Implementation of a backend signing script acting as a proprietary Oracle. This allows the PagoTIC admin to manually input and publish off-chain data (visualizations/royalties) onto the blockchain.
  3. Testnet PagoTic - PayoutEvent: Execution of on-chain transactions where the Trusted Publisher records distributed payments (Payouts) using Metadata Label 674 (Proof of Payment).
  4. End-to-end smoke path on testnet.
  5. ﻿Unit and integration tests implemented and executed in the CI pipeline.
title: Smart Contracts on testnet and traceable royalties

  3. All backoffice flows operate on testnet; manual transfer to a verified wallet succeeds; holders view is accurate.
  4. Internal build available; tokens and metadata are visible from testnet sources.
  5. The system successfully creates on-chain transactions containing specific metadata (Label 674) linked to the users' verified wallets; these transactions serve as immutable proof that the off-chain Fiat payment was triggered/completed.ç
  6. ﻿Documented validation where Artists confirm Backoffice functionality and Token Holders confirm Mobile App usability. At least 70% of participants rate the experience as “clear” or “very clear” in a short survey; their qualitative comments are captured in the Artist Feedback Report and Token Holder Feedback Report.
description:

  2. Alpha web dashboard reading testnet chain (balances/history/exports).
  3. Backoffice (testnet): add work/album, mint CIP-68, update metadata, transfers to verified wallets, holders view.

  5. Testnet Payout Attestation: Execution of a "Proof of Payment" dry-run. Since actual payouts are processed in Fiat by PagoTic (off-chain) due to regulatory compliance, the system generates On-chain Attestations using Metadata Label 674 to record and witness the payout event for ≥5 verified wallets.

acceptance_criteria:
1. Critical Data Mapping: there is clear evidence of critical data events mapped for target gold mining supply-chain. Critical data events refer to the key sequences along the supply-chain (i.e the end to end process mapping) from extraction, processing, refining, tokenization and redemption. Under each event, there should be a clear list of different data required to be captured (for example with extraction it would relate to the date, mine location, quantities, timestamps).
  2. Document covering the technical and operational feasibility / scope for the core functions of this proposal. It should cover chapters on:
  3. Traceability across the core supply-chain sequences (e.g which parts of the chain to trace, which ones not to and why).
  4. Tokenization (which CIP standards to use and why. Breakdown on the trade offs on these approach).
  5. Proof of Reserves
  6. Redemption process.
  7. In pdf format, there is a document outlining the metadata requirements for the traceable mineral assets (detailed what is stored on IPFS and within the token metadata).
  8. Draft tokenization logic includes mint/burn and reserve reconciliation steps (these are not smart contracts but the general logic of how the transaction is built, executed and flows based on the various events).
  9. At least 2–3 candidate custodians shortlisted with documented evaluation criteria (will be used to start initial discussions and terms).
  10. DeFi integration framework specifies use cases, compatible protocols, and liquidity pathways. Minimum of 5 Cardano Defi protocols analysed for integration potential. Each analysis should outline the benefits to the Cardano community and mining project as well specify what the integration could look like.

acceptance_criteria:
Reviewers should first confirm each monthly report submission for the months listed in the Outputs section: posted as dated files at github.com/rphair/cip-editing.

Reviewers can then confirm these monthly report sections:

  • A "Quantitative" section near the beginning which contains two clickable lists (pull requests and issues) of all current GitHub CIP threads that the proposer has been directly involved in (though review, commentary, or issue resolution)
  • A "Quantitative" section with hand-written summaries of the proposer's less standard activities of this monthly period, including: unique, high-level issues of the CIP process as a whole; community events, activities & posted documents; and any "Spontaneous activities" and "Maintenance projects" as defined in the milestone outputs & proposal document
  • The review section "Work on pull requests" (plus the similar but less used "issues & discussions") with sections of bullet points for the key CIP documents the proposer has personally progressed in this monthly period
  • Evidence of each CIP meeting held, including for each one: its sequential meeting number, its date & time, the link to its agenda, its most significant discussion points, and any tangible changes (merged CIPs) resulting from that meeting

Reviewers can additionally verify the proposer's work history in Work on pull requests as:

  • Each key CIP review item — chosen by the proposer as the most significant for this monthly period, out of the greater number of active pull requests on GitHub — begins with its pull request number and latest title.
  • This item contains a bulleted list of the most significant steps in review, discussion or "merge" (inclusion in the CIP repository) that the proposer has personally posted as a GitHub comment, action or review.
  • The first part of each bullet point is generally the proposer's summary of the progress that was made: a one-line comment explicit enough for reviewers to understand what the proposer has helped achieve but concise enough to keep the level of detail easily reviewable.
  • The second part is a verification link, which reviewers can click to verify that the proposer has been directly involved in that production: through its authorship, date & time, and context recorded and clearly visible on GitHub.
  • (Note: if links to others' comments or actions are occasionally made, these would also be considered important as responses that have been achieved indirectly through the proposer's own review, activity and commentary that surrounds it.)

The acceptance criteria for monthly reporting is the same for all 3 milestones.

description:
Output 1: Based on the DAO concept document, the coordinator creates the low-level design that will contain:

The roles that can use the platform and their rights will be described:

* viewers - anyone with a Cardano wallet can see the data,

* DReps - can freely log in at any time and start voting on proposals,

* submitters - after meeting the entry conditions (to be defined in milestone 1), they can submit proposals


Description of principles: The entry rules for all roles will be described in detail. The basic rules of the DAO will be described - i.e., the DAO mission, voting rules, deadlines, form of communication with teams, responsibility for the operation of the platform, form of voting, publication of results, and distribution of funds.

At this stage, the team will know what funding method the DReps have agreed on. The team will research and propose a plan to implement the funding process (distribution). It can be on-chain, via Intersect, or other methods.

Flow charts and diagrams: The life cycle of roles will be defined (e.g., how a DRep can opt in and out of the DAO), the life cycle of proposals from submission to distribution of funds (or rejection), the voting process, the funding process (it is not certain at this time whether funds will be distributed via SC, via Intersect, or in another form).


The database tables: List of tables and their basic items and relationships.


Considering the use of existing technologies:

* Technologies used for the front-end.

* Technologies used for voting (existing on-chain voting system or off-chain voting with an on-chain anchor).

* Distribution of funds (existing SC, new SC, collaboration with Intersect or other entity).


Output 2: Milestone report detailing the progress and results.
title: Low-level design of DAO

  4. Specification
  5. Rationale: how does this CIP achieve its goals?
  6. Path to Active

  10. The document of the domain separation logic for typed structured data signing should contain a definition of the domain separation logic that is specifically designed to supply the Cardano address format and UTxO model. The definition should clearly include: how the cardano network domains are separated (preprod / mainnet / testnet) in the message structure, and also how this message is represented in utxo based transactions.
  11. The document of the supported types and encoding rules and security considerations should specifically address:
  12. Supported types
  13. Encoding rules
  14. The following security considerations (replay protection, type safety).

acceptance_criteria:

Correctness against reference: Given an immutable block database, the library is able to successfully process all blocks contained in the database. This is validated against the latest version of cardano-db-tool available at the time of PoA submission. Immutable database samples are provided and used as part of the test suite for reproducibility.

On a baseline machine (8 CPU cores and 16 GB of RAM), the block streaming interface of the immutable database streams block data at ≥ 150k blocks/min with Resident Set ≤ 1.5 GiB. The benchmarks are executable with `cargo bench` and benchmark reports are available & regenerable.

acceptance_criteria:
Correctness & Robustness of all 3 components:

Peer manager: From a clean start with a list of bootstrap peers provided, the peer manager is able to maintain connections with a configurable amount of peers. This will be ensured by conducting prolonged tests on preview and preprod testnets, and providing logs collected during the experimentation. A locally reproducible simulation will also be made available. This simulation will support dropping arbitrary messages, and will also simulate the loss of peer connections. The simulation report along with peer-manager logs will also be generable.

Chain synchronizer: From any provided point on the block-chain, the chain-sync module is able to reach the latest tip within 5 minutes. Multi-day tests will be conducted on testnet, and the logs will be available. The correctness of the chain synchronizer is verifiable against the latest cardano-node version at the time of PoA submission locally through simulations. Local simulations are also used to prove that the chain-sync component is able to withstand rollbacks of arbitrary sizes. This is verifiable through simulation reports that can be generated locally.

Block fetcher: The block fetcher component is able to download arbitrary ranges of blocks at ≥ 20k blocks/min. All blocks are verifiably valid against the accepted block-chain, which can be access through Mithril. The relevant subset of blocks will also be provided in the Github Release.


Composability & resource bounds:

An example within the repository shows the use of all three modules together. This example is reproducible on preprod, and demonstrates that the latest chain tip is reached while also storing blocks to a file, and maintaining connection with a configurable set of peers. Block header hashes and block integrity are verified once the partial node has successfully shutdown. The partial node maintains steady-state RSS ≤ 600 MiB and CPU ≤ 150% throughout a 30 minute run, on a machine with 8 CPU cores and 16 GB of RAM.

All protocol versions and software versions used are pinned, and documented as part of reviewer documentation for the milestone.
description:
A new crate within the pallas-extras workspace providing composable, asynchronous building blocks for interacting with Cardano’s node-to-node networking layer. The peer manager will:

  • Maintain the Handshake, Peer Sharing, and optionally Keep-Alive mini-protocols.
  • Maintain a dynamic list of active and available peers.
  • Provide APIs to manage connections and peer discovery.

The chain syncrhonizer will:

  • Maintain the Chain Sync mini-protocol, keeping a valid state of the current blockchain block headers in memory.
  • Allow syncing of block headers from upstream peers.
  • Emit a stream of new tip updates or rollbacks.

The block fetcher will:

  • Fetch blocks from upstream peers using the Block Fetch mini protocol.
  • Request full blocks based on chain state.
  • Send blocks to downstream peers on request.

As for both previous milestones, proper documentation will be enforced along with high test coverage.

Each component will be implemented as an independent asynchronous actor, composable with other components. CI with automated testing, formatting, and linting will also be implemented.
title: Network Components Module

The deliverable for this milestone is the core Hydra Hub web platform, consisting of two main components:

  • Consumer Portal – A user interface for developers or end-users to register an account, securely authenticate, and submit requests for Hydra node access. The portal will include account management, profile editing, and the ability to submit usage requests with a description of the intended dApp testing purpose. The system will support multiple devices (desktop, mobile) and feature a friendly, easy-to-use interface.
  • Admin Dashboard – An interface for Hydra Hub administrators to review requests, allocate nodes, monitor node status, track system performance, and manage the entire consumer list. The dashboard will include functions to display activity logs, real-time node status reports, and manage allocation history.

In addition, the system will incorporate strict authentication and role-based access control to ensure a clear separation of functions between consumers and admins. All functions will be programmed for scalability to support a decentralized model in later phases

description:
1.Smart Contract Development (Aiken)

Develop a payment smart contract using Aiken (Plutus V3).

Contract logic:

  • A consumer clicks “Buy Hydra Node” in the Hydra Hub portal.
  • The backend builds a transaction embedding node and user metadata.
  • The consumer signs and submits the transaction, paying the service fee.
  • Upon confirmation, Hydra Hub automatically issues an API key granting node access.

2.Admin Claim & Refund Mechanism

The admin address can claim the payment after 1 day (24-hour delay).

During the dispute period (1 day), if the user and admin reach agreement (via email or GitHub issue), the admin can issue a refund to the user from the contract.

3.Integration with Hydra Hub

Integrate the smart contract endpoints with the Hydra Hub backend and dashboard, displaying:

  • Payment status
  • Remaining usage period
  • Service suspension upon expiry

4.Dashboard Update

Extend Admin and Consumer dashboards to show transaction records, payment status, and claim/refund logs.

5.Testing

Test all core transaction flows:

  • buy – User purchases and pays successfully
  • refund – Admin refunds within dispute window
  • claim – Admin claims payment after 1 day

acceptance_criteria:
A1. The specification removes all post-dated transactions in Hydrozoa’s design, replacing them with corresponding observer-script based mechanisms. Specifically, the following post-dated transactions will be replaced:

  • Post-dated refund transactions (which return deposits that the head hasn’t absorbed in time)
  • Post-dated fallback transactions (which transition the head to the rule-based regime if the head’s L1 state has not been modified in a while – which indicates multisig consensus failure)

B1. The prototype implements the specified observer-script based mechanisms replacing:

  • Post-dated refund transactions
  • Post-dated fallback transactions

C1. Documentation describes the prototype and how to run it.

NOTE TO REVIEWERS: Regarding CIP-112 (https://cips.cardano.org/cip/CIP-0112). The Cardano ledger repository (https://github.com/IntersectMBO/cardano-ledger) already has a draft implementation of the CIP which would be suitable for Hydrozoa’s prototyping. The Plutus repository has not progressed very far in the CIP-112 implementation (https://github.com/IntersectMBO/plutus/issues/7342), but we are hopeful that progress will pick up now that the inter-era hardfork is implemented. Note that we don’t actually need a hardfork covering CIP-112 to reach Cardano mainnet – we only need a draft implementation corresponding to the specification in CIP-112.

However, if it turns out that the Plutus implementation of CIP-112 is not ready by the time we need to start work on this milestone, we still have options. The Scalus (https://scalus.org/) that we’re already using in Hydrozoa provides flexibility to modify the ledger rules and plutus script context. Thus, we will implement CIP-112 in Scalus to enable our prototype of CIP-112 based Hydrozoa features.

*Clarification:

In response to the Catalyst Team reviewer’s questions, we would like to offer the following clarifications:

1. Fujitsu’s role and dependencies

As described in our proposal, Fujitsu’s role in the overall project (not tied specifically to Milestone 1) is to provide access to athlete(s) and their mocap-AI technology, enabling Anifie to generate motion-based NFTs using Fujitsu's mocap-AI on the athletes provided by Fujitsu.

However, Milestones 1–6 (Final Milestone) do not depend on Fujitsu’s athlete delivery. These milestones allow us to create communities for artists, athletes, and/or enterprises. Therefore, even if Fujitsu does not provide athletes during a given milestone period, Anifie can fully satisfy milestone requirements through communities of artists or enterprises (or even athletes that Anifie brings without Fujitsu).

That said, Fujitsu and Anifie successfully created a chat community at the World Championship Gymnastics in late October 2025, where we created and sold NFTs from motion data of world-renowned gymnasts using Fujitsu’s mocap-AI.

Please see the public links here:

https://bit.ly/4p56AUI

https://bit.ly/4r12Ghx

Had Catalyst approval been granted by that time, this real-world traction could have been reflected in Milestone 1.

2. Project manager clarification

For Milestone 1, the approval for the test results from the quality assurance member will be provided by Yohei Iwasaki of Anifie Japan - not Fujitsu.

As stated in the proposal, the project is managed by:

  • Yohei Iwasaki, CEO of Anifie Japan, who provides overall oversight and directly manages John Oetjen; and
  • John Oetjen, a Grammy Award–winning artist on our team and also manages the project. For clarity, John will not approve the test results from the quality assurance member regarding Milestone 1.

Fujitsu does not serve as a project manager for this Catalyst project (unlike John or Yohei, Fujitsu is not listed as a project manager in the proposal at all).

3. Community planned for Milestone 1

For Milestone 1, our current plan is to create a community within the product for Imari Tones, a Christian heavy-metal band from Japan with a global fanbase.

However, to avoid creating any dependencies, if for any reason this community becomes unsuitable, we will instead create a qualifying community for an artist, an athlete, or an enterprise—all of which are permitted under the milestone criteria.


**Further clarification applicable to all milestones from Milestone 1 through the Final Milestone, wherever applicable:

acceptance_criteria:
• Specification Published: The final, comprehensive Architecture Specification Document is publicly published, detailing the required APIs, data models, and cryptographic standards for Agent binding, issuance, and verification.
  • Wallet Binding Defined: The specification contains the complete, formal definition of the Wallet Binding Flow, including required on-chain auditable event structures (if applicable).
  • VC Verification Defined: The specification contains the complete, formal definition of the Credential Verification Flow, including required schemas (e.g., for Agent Reputation VCs) and cryptographic verification steps.
description:
Development of a comprehensive Architecture Specification Document that enables AI Agents on the Masumi Network to leverage existing Decentralized Identity (DID) standards (W3C DID, Verifiable Credentials, KERI) without reinventing identity models. This specification will formally define the required interfaces for:

  1. How agents bind DIDs to their wallets.
  2. How identity is verified across agent interactions.
  3. How Verifiable Credentials (VCs) such as reputation, compliance status (e.g., KYC/KYB), or technical expertise are issued and consumed.

The specification will provide the foundation for agent discovery, trust, and reputational systems across the ecosystem.

Scope Clarification

This milestone delivers the complete, finalized specification document.

  • Specification (Specs): A formal document defining the complete architecture, data models, and API endpoints for the Agent Identity Framework.
  • Identity Flows Detailed: The specification will fully define the following critical flows:
  • Wallet Binding Flow: The full cryptographic and API sequence for linking a Masumi Agent's wallet to a W3C DID or KERI identifier.

  • Credential Verification Flow: The full API sequence, data structure (schemas), and cryptographic requirements for an Agent to request and successfully verify a Verifiable Credential (VC) issued by a third party, with a focus on Agent Reputation VCs.
title: Milestone 1: Identity Integration Framework

acceptance_criteria:
• Multi-Language SDK Availability: The Masumi Identity SDK is released and publicly available in Python (e.g., via PyPI) and/or JavaScript/TypeScript (e.g., via npm).
  • Core API Functionality: The SDK in both languages contains functions that successfully perform:
  • Linking a Masumi Agent wallet to a DID/KERI identifier.
  • Requesting and verifying a Verifiable Credential (VC) in an agent-to-agent interaction.
  • Documentation: All required documentation is published, including API reference documentation, step-by-step tutorials, and developer onboarding guides.
  • External Integration Verified: At least one external developer/team successfully integrates the released SDK into their own, independent AI agent or application, verifying usability.
description:
Release of developer-friendly SDKs and tooling that make it easy to embed DID functionality and credential verification into agents, lowering the barrier for adoption. These SDKs will abstract away the complexity of DID resolution and credential verification, providing ready-to-use APIs for linking agents to DIDs (or potentially other Identity Standards), and requesting/verifying them during agent-to-agent interactions. 

The SDK will come with documentation, tutorials, and onboarding guides, ensuring that any developer can add trusted identity to their agents in minutes rather than weeks.

Scope Details:

  • Supported Languages: The SDK is delivered in at least one major programming language: Python and/or JavaScript/TypeScript.
  • APIs Included: APIs for linking agents to identities, and core functions to request, hold, and verify VCs during A2A interactions.
  • Templates Included: The release includes a template agent application for each supported language to demonstrate out-of-the-box identity integration.
title: Milestone 2: Developer SDK for Agent Identity

acceptance_criteria:

  • Prototype Testnet Operational: An L2 prototype testnet is deployed, live, and successfully connected to the Masumi Network L1.
  • Performance Target 1 (Throughput): The L2 prototype successfully demonstrates a sustained throughput of at least 500+ agent-to-agent transactions per second (TPS) in a benchmark test.
  • Performance Target 2 (Efficiency): The prototype demonstrates that agent payments executed on L2 have a latency of less than 500 milliseconds (ms) and a transaction fee reduction of at least 90% compared to a standard Cardano L1 transaction.
  • Monitoring Dashboards Ready: Basic monitoring dashboards for tracking performance metrics similar to L2 throughput, latency, and costs are fully deployed and functional.
description: Design and implementation of a dedicated Layer 2 prototype optimized for the unique requirements of the AI Agent economy, where billions of microtransactions and high-frequency interactions will occur. The prototype will demonstrate how Hydra channels, optimistic rollups, or similar scaling technologies can enable agents to transact at a fraction of the cost and latency of L1. It will include a developer-accessible testnet, transaction monitoring dashboards, and performance benchmarks to validate that the L2 can handle large-scale throughput (e.g., thousands of agent transactions per second).
title: Milestone 3: L2 Architecture & Prototype

acceptance_criteria:
• Identity Retention Success: Test transactions executed on the L2 mainnet and testnet are successfully tied to the Masumi Agent's existing DID/KERI identity, verified through the L2 audit log.
  • Settlement Verification Success: The final L2-to-L1 settlement mechanism successfully processes 50 of 50 consecutive settlement transactions (deposits/withdrawals/closures) to a Cardano testnet successfully without any loss of funds on mainnet and testnet.
  • Performance Retention: L2 transaction latency and cost metrics, as defined in M3, are maintained Latency <500ms, Transaction Cost Reduction 95% during the integration tests.
  • SDK/API Compatibility: All core L1 functions within the existing Masumi SDKs/APIs successfully execute L2 transactions without requiring developers to change more than the configuration endpoint.
description:
Full technical integration of the operational Layer 2 system (from M3) with the existing Masumi Network Mainnet and Testnet. This integration delivers a frictionless developer experience by ensuring L2 usage is indistinguishable from L1 usage via existing Masumi tools.

Integration Scope:

  1. Wallet Operations: All Masumi Agent wallet functions (send, receive, balance checks) are fully functional on the L2 system via the existing L1 APIs/SDKs.
  2. Agent Identity Flow: The DID/KERI identity framework and credential verification flows are fully integrated and functional on the L2, ensuring agents retain their trust profile during L2 transactions.
  3. Secure Settlement: The final mechanism for trustless and secure settlement of funds/data between L2 and the Cardano L1 is implemented, including handling for common settlement edge cases (e.g., channel closures, timeout conditions).
title: Milestone 4: L2/Scaling Integration with Masumi

acceptance_criteria:
• At least 3 external developers or businesses integrate DID + L2 functionality into their agents.
  • Agents verify identity/credentials before transacting on L2.
  • Demonstration of a real workflow requiring both trust and high-frequency payments (e.g., marketplace transactions, data exchange, API calls) on mainnet and testnet.
  • Performance validated with at least 10,000 transactions in a 24h window.
  • L1 Settlement mainnet and testnet
description:
A real-world pilot program demonstrating how trusted, identity-aware agents can transact at scale using Masumi’s integrated identity framework and Layer 2 payments on mainnet and testnet. The pilot will showcase agents verifying each other’s credentials before engaging in high-frequency transactions on L2, proving both trust and sacalability in practice. It will involve external developers and businesses deploying real agents in workflows such as marketplaces, data exchanges, or autonomous API economies. The pilot will provide not only a technical demonstration but also case studies and performance metrics, proving that the Masumi Network can serve as the backbone for a global agent economy.

Specific Pilot Boundaries:

  1. Industry Focus: The pilot agents used will be for the Marketing, Media, or Data Science, or Research industries.
  2. Transaction Type: The pilot will validate autonomous API subscription and/or high-frequency data exchange agent-to-agent microtransactions.
  3. Integration Depth: External agents must utilize the Masumi SDK to perform three specific actions: (a) Agent Wallet Binding, (b) DID/Credential Verification of a Counterparty, and (c) L2 Microtransaction Execution and L1 Settlement.
title: Milestone 5: Unified Identity + L2/Scaling Pilot

description:

  • These abstractions tables can include token/native transfers, token balances and higher-level datasets, e.g., token and native token (ADA) transfers partitioned by sender address and receiver address.
  • The exact set of abstraction tables will be determined during implementation, based on Cardano’s UTxO data structure, data volume characteristics, and the most efficient way to compute the required standardized metrics. All abstraction tables created will be fully documented and shared with Milestone Reviewers for verification.
  • These data tables are used in the calculation of metrics such as Transaction count and Daily Active Users (DAU).

description:
Establish the foundation of our UPLC evaluation engine by building a comprehensive parser capable of reading and interpreting flat-encoded UPLC bytecode as it exists on the Cardano blockchain. This parser transforms raw bytecode into structured abstract syntax trees (ASTs) for CEK machine evaluation. 

1. Source code containing:  

  • Complete UPLC parser supporting UPLC constructs (Lambda, Apply, Const, Builtin, Delay, Force, Error)  
  • AST data structures  
  • Validation logic ensuring scripts are well-formed with comprehensive error reporting  

2. Short technical note describing how the parser works

Good day, Reviewers! We greatly appreciate your thoughtful feedback and share your commitment to maintaining high-quality project standards.

After reviewing our initial Statement of Milestones, we decided it would be most effective to focus each milestone on one major aspect of development. For Milestone 1, our priority is the parser implementation itself — ensuring it includes the outputs listed above.

At this stage, the design is reflected in the code structure, allowing us to concentrate on functionality and correctness rather than separate design documentation. The source code will therefore serve as the verifiable output, directly accessible for review.

While testing is already covered under the parser’s validation logic, formal unit testing and documentation have been scheduled for Milestone 3, where comprehensive validation will be conducted through comparison with the Aiken UPLC test suite. We believe this sequencing provides a clearer and more efficient workflow, and we hope the reviewers will kindly consider this approach.
title: UPLC Parser Implementation (Months 1-2)

description:

  • Resource limit enforcement tracking memory usage, CPU steps, and stack depth

2. Short technical note describing how the CEK machine works

Good day, Reviewers!

Thank you for your continued feedback on our milestones.

Similar to Milestone 1, this phase focuses on implementation, specifically the core CEK (Control, Environment, Kontinuation) machine. At this stage, our goal is to deliver a fully functional CEK core with proper resource handling, error propagation, and debugging as outlined above.

Formal documentation and testing artifacts will then be consolidated in Milestone 3, where both the parser and CEK machine will undergo conformance testing using the Aiken UPLC test suite.

For this milestone, reviewers will be able to verify functionality directly through the source code.

Thank you once again and we hope you have a great day!

This stage will also involve testing against the official Aiken UPLC test suite, ensuring that the integrated parser and CEK machine conform to expected Plutus semantics and produce consistent results with the Aiken reference implementation.

A health-check or metadata document ( $metadata ) is reachable, confirming the service is up.

  3. Transaction Lookup: Given a transaction hash, the service returns the transaction details (inputs, outputs, metadata).
  4. Address Balance: Given a Cardano address, the service returns the current ADA balance and asset list for that address.
  5. Metadata Query: Given an identifier (e.g. transaction hash or asset ID), the service returns associated metadata (transaction metadata or token metadata as applicable).

  7. Schema Compliance: All OData responses conform to the defined EDMX (Odata) schema and include all required fields for their entity type. For example, a transaction query returns fields like transaction hash, timestamp, inputs/outputs, etc., matching the documentation. Any filtering or pagination follows OData standards.
  8. Error Handling: The service handles error conditions with clear, standardized responses. At minimum, five distinct error scenarios are covered: (1) invalid input format (e.g. malformed address or hash) results in an HTTP 400 response with descriptive error message; (2) data not found (e.g. unknown transaction hash) returns a 404-style OData error; (3) Cardano API connectivity failure (timeout or API down) returns a 503 error with retry advice; (4) unauthorized access (if endpoints are secured) returns HTTP 401/403; (5) any internal server error is trapped and returns a generic error response without crashing the service.
  9. Open Source Code Availability: The codebase is publicly available in the GitHub repository under the Apache 2.0 license. Repository includes a clear commit history and issues/README indicating this milestone’s completion.
  10. Test Coverage: Automated tests cover at least 70% of the code relevant to this milestone’s functionality. The test suite includes at least 15 test cases that cover typical successful queries (e.g. valid transaction fetch), edge cases (e.g. empty results, large responses), and error scenarios (as listed above). All tests pass in continuous integration, providing objective evidence of correctness.
  11. Demonstration Query: A sample end-to-end demonstration (for instance, querying a known test transaction via the OData service) succeeds with the expected result. The query completes within an acceptable time (< 5 seconds) and the returned data matches the actual blockchain data, confirming the integration works in real time.

acceptance_criteria:
1. Transaction Construction: The API is capable of constructing a Cardano transaction from specified input parameters. At minimum, given a destination address and an ADA amount (and optionally metadata), the system produces a well-formed unsigned transaction. The transaction includes correct inputs and outputs and a valid fee, such that it passes basic validation from Cardano CLI’s transaction verification.
  2. Protocol Compliance: The constructed unsigned transaction adheres to Cardano protocol rules. This means, for example, the sum of inputs covers outputs + fees, no invalid UTXO usage, and the CBOR format is correct. Verification: gets acepted after signed and submitted.
  3. External Signing & Submission: A signed transaction (produced by signing the API’s unsigned transaction externally) is successfully submitted to the Cardano testnet and achieves confirmation. Specifically, at least one preview test transaction built by the system, when signed with a valid key, is accepted by the network (appearing on a Cardano testnet explorer with ≥1 confirmation).
  4. Error Handling (Transaction Flow): The system handles transaction-related errors with clear outcomes. At minimum, five error scenarios are implemented and documented:
  5. Insufficient funds – if the provided UTXOs or source address balance can’t cover the transaction amount and fees, the build process fails with a clear error message;
  6. Invalid input data – e.g. malformed address or amount out of range yields a 400-level error;
  7. Invalid signature – if a submitted transaction is signed with the wrong key or tampered, the submit action returns a failure (and the error is logged/reported);
  8. Network failure – if the submission endpoint times out or is unreachable, the service returns an error indicating a submit failure (and does not crash);
  9. Duplicate or Replay – if the same transaction is submitted twice, the service handles the error from the node (already processed transaction). All such conditions have corresponding error codes/messages defined in the docs
  10. Open Source & Transparency: All new code for the transaction builder and submitter is committed to the public repository (Apache 2.0). The documentation in the repo is updated to reflect the Milestone 2 features (transaction building/signing/submission). Reviewers can find a clear changelog or milestone tag indicating what was added.
  11. Demonstration Scenario: A demo scenario is executed to validate this milestone: for example, “Send 10 ADA on preview testnet from Address A to Address B.” Using the API, a transaction is built, externally signed, then submitted. Acceptance is achieved if the transaction is visible on the testnet blockchain (with the correct amount transferred) and the OData service/API reflects a successful submission. The entire process should be reproducible using the provided scripts or instructions
description:
1. Transaction Builder Module: Implementation of a server-side module within the CAP service that can construct a raw Cardano transaction from given API inputs. This builder supports at least basic ADA transfer transactions with optional metadata. It handles UTXO selection and fee calculation using existing Cardano libraries (cardano-serialization-lib , mesh.js, lucid-evolution etc. ). The output of this module is an unsigned transaction in CBOR serialized format ready to be signed.
  2. Transaction Submission Functionality: Integration with the Cardano-Connector Module from M1 to submit a signed transaction. Using a preview API (Blockfrost or Koios’s submit endpoint), the service can take a signed transaction blob and broadcast it to the Cardano preview testnet. This output includes handling the network response and tracking the submission result (transaction ID).
  3. End-to-End Example Scripts: Reference implementation or scripts that demonstrate the full build–sign–submit flow. For instance, a sample script that calls the OData API to build a transaction, then invokes an external signing step (outside the CAP service), and calls the submit endpoint of the API to broadcast the transaction.
  4. Extended Documentation: Updates to the documentation (/docs) focusing on transaction handling. This includes a Transaction Schema Specification (what inputs are required for transaction building, format of the unsigned transaction), a Signing Workflow Guide (how an external party should sign the transaction), with examples using Cardano CLI or similar), and a Troubleshooting & Error Codes section for common issues like insufficient funds, invalid inputs or other submission failures.
  5. Test Cases for Build/Submit: Additional automated tests are developed to validate the transaction builder logic. One or more unit test to construct a transaction with known inputs and verify the structure or fee, and an integration test simulating submission with a dummy signature to ensure the flow is working up to the submission call.
title: Transaction Build & Submit

  2. Private-Key Isolation Confirmed: CAP service never stores or uses private key material (code review + architecture evidence).
  3. SAP Integration Operational: An SAP process can trigger an API call and receive data or transaction confirmation within 10 seconds.
  4. Wallet Viewer App Functional: Working SAP Fiori application that displays wallet information through OData services, including filtered views for balances, tokens, and transaction history.

description:
1. Unsigned Transaction Export Interface: Extension of the transaction module to support exporting unsigned transactions for external signing. The OData Action BuildTransaction returns a vailid payload containing a deterministic reference id, hash placeholder and timestamp. This enables third-party signers (Cardano CLI, Browser Wallets etc.) to sign externally – no private keys handled in the CAP service.
  2. External Signer Integration Module: Implementation of the external signing workflow using the Cardano CLI as reference signer. Flow: Unsigned TX → External Sign → Verify → Assemble → Submit. Demonstrates full round-trip signing with complete key separation and no private-key exposure
  3. SAP Business Process Integration Examples: Examples for Integration of the Cardano OData API into an SAP S/4HANA process (for example, a Purchase Order posting triggers a Cardano transaction or retrieves on-chain data).
  4. Extended Enterprise Use Cases: Enterprise Use Cases: Exampels of advanced real-world SAP scenarios based on the integration: (e.g., sustainability tracking of CO₂ certificates, tokenized inter-company settlements, audit-trail reporting for FI/CO documents). Each use case includes ABAP examples and SAP/Explorer screenshots.
  5. Basic Wallet Viewer Fiori Sample App: A lightweight SAPUI5/Fiori application that visualizes wallet information from the OData API which demonstrates how easy it is to build simple apps based on the Odataservices / CAP definitions and can be used as a reference in future applications.  
  6.  Automated Integration & Security Tests: ≥ 15 automated tests covering external signing, signature validation, SAP integration, and error conditions.

  • Deserialize → (no-op) → reserialize is demonstrated by tests to preserve ledger-relevant semantics (same inputs spent, outputs/values, fees, validity interval, mint/burn, withdrawals/certs, required signers, collateral, script integrity, metadata/datum refs). Re-serialization era may differ; semantics must not. No-op tests will include at least a single test that uses each transaction field. Semantic equivalence will be tested by parsing the final cbor with Pallas and inspected. (All tests pass; no panics.)
  • Edit & rebuild with automatic balancing
  • Tests show common edit scenarios (changing outputs/amounts, metadata, validity interval, required signers) rebuild into balanced transactions with recalculated fees. Invalid edits produce typed/structured errors rather than crashes. Transaction edit tests will include common scenarios, it isn’t possible to cover all possible edit scenarios, at least a single test will be included for editing every field in a transaction. Semantic equivalence will be tested by parsing the final cbor with Pallas and inspected.
  • Utils parity after migration
  • Golden-vector tests demonstrate that each ported util produces the same results as the prior whisky-csl version (or documents any intentional differences and why).
  • Release & documentation quality
  • The tagged release is published with notes describing the new parser/edit/rebuild flow and utils migration; README quick-start/examples are updated and runnable; the X post and Discord announcement link to the release and docs.
description:
• TxParser (Pallas-based) for decode → edit → rebuild
  • APIs to parse transaction CBOR, expose fields for safe mutation, and rebuild a transaction body with a helper that re-balances change and recalculates fees.
  • Transaction editing workflow
  • Ability to deserialize a transaction, read the relevant fields (e.g., inputs/outputs, metadata, validity interval, required signers), apply user edits, and rebuild with the TxBuilder.
  • Port whisky-csl utils to Pallas
  • Drop-in replacements for the existing CSL-backed helpers (e.g., key-hash → bech32 address, script hash extraction from Native/Plutus CBOR, DRep ID from key hashes).
  • Public release & docs/announcements
  • ﻿GitHub tag/release with notes summarising the parser/edit/rebuild capability and the utils migration; README examples updated; one X (Twitter) post and one Discord announcement linking to the release and docs.
title: Development of Whisky-pallas Phase 2

acceptance_criteria:

  • Publication criteria: Release exists in https://github.com/sidan-lab/whisky; README/examples and possibly MIGRATION.md are present at the tagged commit; Twitter/X and Discord announcements link to the tag
description:
• Refactor all remaining components previously using CSL to use Pallas instead in https://github.com/sidan-lab/whisky/tree/master/packages/whisky-csl .

Any such changes should be documented and migration instructions given in MIGRATION.md in https://github.com/sidan-lab/whisky/tree/master/packages/whisky-csl

title: Full migration from whisky-csl to whisky-pallas
